[THOUGHT]  
This is a young adult with acute, progressive DIP joint pain and swelling following a non-penetrating but forceful traumatic injury (jersey pull), without signs of cellulitis or skin breach. The absence of erythema, warmth, or systemic symptoms makes classic sepsis less likely *at first glance*, but septic arthritis remains the top concern because: (1) the DIP joint is a small, relatively avascular joint highly susceptible to hematogenous or direct inoculation; (2) even minor trauma can introduce skin flora (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*) into the joint space via microtears or transient synovial breach; (3) progression over 48 hours despite no fracture/dislocation strongly suggests an active intra-articular process — and in the absence of mechanical symptoms or clear soft-tissue hematoma on X-ray, infection is the most dangerous and time-sensitive diagnosis to rule out. While early flexor tenosynovitis is considered, Kanavel signs (fusiform swelling, tenderness along tendon sheath, pain on passive extension, and flexed posture) are explicitly absent, and the swelling is localized *to the DIP joint*, not the flexor tendon sheath (which would center over the proximal/middle phalanx). Post-traumatic inflammatory synovitis or hematoma is possible, but typically plateaus or improves within 24–48 hours — not worsens progressively. Critically, the diagnostic plan correctly prioritizes *joint aspiration before antibiotics*, which is the gold-standard step to confirm or exclude septic arthritis. Pending labs and POCUS are supportive but cannot replace synovial fluid analysis for definitive diagnosis.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive pain and swelling localized specifically to the DIP joint over 48 hours  
- History of forceful non-penetrating trauma (jersey entanglement/pull) — mechanism capable of introducing inoculum or disrupting synovial integrity  
- X-ray shows no fracture or dislocation, but confirms soft tissue swelling at the DIP joint — consistent with intra-articular pathology  
- No erythema, warmth, or skin breach — does not exclude septic arthritis (especially early or immunocompetent hosts)  
- Absence of mechanical symptoms (stiffness, locking, catching) argues against chronic or structural joint disease  
- Clinical suspicion high enough to warrant urgent joint aspiration prior to antibiotics — standard-of-care for suspected septic arthritis  

[GAPS]  
- Synovial fluid analysis results (WBC count/differential, Gram stain, culture) — definitive for septic arthritis  
- CRP and ESR values — elevated acute-phase reactants would support inflammatory/infectious etiology  
- POCUS findings — presence/absence of hypoechoic joint effusion, hypervascularity (power Doppler), or loculations would further support or challenge septic arthritis  
- Blood culture results — though often negative in native-joint septic arthritis, positive cultures would confirm diagnosis  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Septic arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joint
